sections.heading: Three categories in one borderland
paras: Ovseichik’s material, from the Vitebsk, Pskov and Smolensk regions, centres on three groups. Unbaptised children were thought unable to enter paradise and to fly at night asking to be baptised; a symbolic baptism or naming after death is widespread. They were kept out of common cemeteries, a ban the author calls strictly enforced in the first half of the twentieth century. Later records mostly call such children angels.

Suicides, in the same material, were thought to go to the devil, not to the ancestors. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the body was often not washed, was buried in the clothes it died in, with no funeral meal and no church service, and sometimes marked with an aspen stake. Reported burial places include crossroads, swamps, a ditch by the cemetery, hills and forest. Respondents expected drought and storms if a suicide lay in the common cemetery.

Sorcerers were ‘impure’ whatever the manner of death, because the devil was thought to take the soul. They were buried outside the cemetery or by its fence. Radical measures are reported: exhuming the body, cutting off the head and setting it between the legs, driving an aspen stake through the body. The author cites one modern informant for this.

sections.alt: A moonlit stream at night with nude women among the brush on the bank, others in a ring-dance along the water toward a church and a thatched house in mist
sections.caption: Makovsky, 1879. A salon picture of rusalki beside a village; the link between rusalki and the unquiet dead is itself in dispute.
sections.credit: Konstantin Makovsky, public domain; via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Walking dead and literary vampires
paras: Ovseichik reports that sorcerers were believed to walk after death, harming people and drinking their blood, and adds that this is rare in the East Slavic area and more typical of South Slavic vampire lore. The borderland material is mostly about where and how the impure dead were buried, not about what they did once they rose.

The upyr’ of nineteenth-century Russian fiction is another matter. One thesis abstract places the literary vampire as a device used in Russian writing from the eighteenth century on, built on older belief. The atlas keeps the two apart: the field records read for this plate do not describe a figure like the literary vampire, and nothing here is evidence for one.

sections.heading: Zelenin and his critics
paras: Zelenin’s 1916 compilation gathered reports from many provinces under one heading and read them together as a single belief: that the earth does not accept the dead of ‘unnatural’ death, who therefore stay among the living. He tied the category to the rusalki. The sources read for this plate raise three objections.

Ovseichik will not extend the word ‘zalozhnye’ beyond its Vyatka use, because it is absent from Belarusian and other traditions and because burial methods varied. Avdeev, from epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs, argues that the related superstitions are of Christian times and not pagan survivals; only his abstract was read. Baiburin’s critique of reading rites as survivals of an earlier religion is a general objection to the method, not a verdict on Zelenin’s evidence.

What remains usable is the dated record. The local reports in the compilation, such as the ravine burials on plate N and the Semik citations on plate O, are evidence of what someone wrote down, from whom and where. The unifying belief is Zelenin’s construction. Where the record is read here, it is cited by place.

sections.heading: A dispute about where the rule came from
paras: Ethnographers of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries took such burial customs for pagan survivals. A. Avdeev argues the opposite for Muscovite Russia: from sixteenth to early eighteenth-century epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs he finds no obstacle to cemetery burial or regular commemoration of those who died violent deaths, and he holds that the related superstitions arose in Christian times.

This plate has the abstract only. It cannot say how strong Avdeev’s evidence is or how far his conclusion reaches beyond the Muscovite sources. It is placed here so that the pagan-survival reading is not left standing alone.

sections.heading: A rule remembered, 2018–2019
paras: A. Ryko’s fieldwork in the Khislavichi district of the Smolensk region found only remnants of such beliefs. Informants born in the 1930s remember that those who hanged or drowned themselves were not taken to the common cemetery; younger people say they know nothing of it and that the drowned lay in the cemetery. Unbaptised infants were not counted as ‘unclean’ there. No one now says that certain dead can return and harm the living.

Set beside Ovseichik, the two studies cover neighbouring districts and different decades of the same century, and they do not agree on unbaptised children. The author says the findings rest on memory and that it is not clear whether the trend is local.

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: The evidence is one borderland and one district, not all of Russia.
Whether rusalki were dead women, or suicides became them, is not decided here. The older sources that say so are a disputed reading.
Measures against the dead are given only as far as the cited article reports them, and never as instructions.
The drowned of the Volga, the dead of epidemics and war, and the ‘parents’ of Semik are outside this plate and need their own sources.

items: Zelenin’s 1916 essays on those who died ‘unnatural’ deaths and on rusalki, read in the 1995 edition, with his own sources checked.
The full text of Avdeev (2019), and the 2020 historiography by I. Afanasyeva on attitudes to ‘vain’ death in the 15th–17th centuries.
The records of the Polotsk and Pskov university folklore archives that Ovseichik cites, to separate archive material from his own notes.
Whether ‘zalozhnye’ in Vyatka dialect is documented in dialect dictionaries, to confirm the local term independently of Zelenin.

plates.title: THE CALENDAR OF THE DEAD
plates.subtitle: Church Saturdays, a Thursday the Church lacks and a cemetery day today
plates.dek: A table of who named which day of commemoration, in registers kept apart: the Church, the movable Easter calendar, the Komi-Permyak region and today’s cemetery. The parish is an open gap, and the question of origin is left open.
plates.marginal: One church text, one Komi-Permyak comparison, one 2016–17 field study. The pagan-origin story is not used.
plates.location: Church calendar; Komi-Permyak districts; Kostroma and Vladimir regions
plates.tradition: Orthodox church calendar and regional folk practice

sections.heading: The Church’s own list
paras: In a church instructional text, Hieromonk Job (Gumerov) names the Saturdays on which the Church commemorates the dead: Meat Fare Saturday, the second, third and fourth Saturdays of Great Lent, Trinity Saturday and St. Demetrius Saturday. He explains the choice of Saturday by its place as the day of rest, and says the Lenten Saturdays stand in for the daily memorial services that are suspended during the fast.

He gives St. Demetrius Saturday a precise origin: it was set up after the battle of Kulikovo in 1380, with the blessing of Sergius of Radonezh, first for the soldiers who fell and later for all the departed. This is the Church’s account of itself, written by a churchman; it is evidence for what the Church holds, not for what a village did.

sections.kicker: PART II · WHY THE DAYS MOVE
sections.heading: A day counted from Easter
paras: Easter moves from year to year, and the days of commemoration counted from it move with it. A source that says ‘Radonitsa’ or ‘Semik’ is giving a weekday and a week after Easter, not a date of the month. The Church now places Radonitsa on the Tuesday of Thomas week, the ninth day after Easter; that was 14 May in 2024. A reference work of 1913 describes it as falling mostly on the Monday of that week and in some places on the Tuesday, so the day itself varied by place and period.

Semik is the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter. Counting from Easter Sunday, that is the forty-fifth day, and Trinity Saturday falls three days later; the counting is this plate’s arithmetic, not a statement in the sources. Semik has no place in the Church’s calendar, which is why Maltsev’s Komi-Permyak material and the encyclopedia treat it as a folk day.
Julian and Gregorian reckoning add a second layer: a family’s date for the same day can differ from the date in a modern table. This plate gives no dates for any year.

sections.heading: A day the church calendar does not have
paras: G. I. Maltsev records the commemoration days of the Komi-Permyaks: Radonitsa, Semik, Trinity Saturday, and the Saturdays before Pokrov and St. Demetrius. He writes that Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, is absent from the Orthodox calendar, that priests took no part in it in the late nineteenth century and did from the early twentieth. After Zelenin he reports that those dead by unnatural death were commemorated at Semik, and quotes a Kungur saying that they are deaf and blind except on that day.

He also describes a slow move: the Permyaks began to hold this commemoration on the Saturdays of general remembrance, reasoning that prayers would be heard better then. His material is four recordings by one researcher, from a people who are not Russian. The plate uses it only as a regional comparison for a pattern that Russian sources describe.

Read more fully, Maltsev’s article describes a day called dzollun or sharlun, held at the cemetery, where such dead were often buried at the edge. Suicides were also remembered at home, with food set on a water barrel or on the threshold. Families bring pancakes, pies and bread, which may be left on graves or given away. Priests joined in the early twentieth century, and a memorial service is held today in the Kudymkar diocese. The article rests on published sources, on material from the Kungur and Komi Zyuzda districts, and on the author’s own fieldwork in the Yusva, Gayny and Kosa districts between 1995 and 2016.

sections.heading: A cemetery day, 2016–2017
paras: E. G. Chesnokova’s fieldwork in the Kostroma and Vladimir regions found the main cemetery commemoration falling in either the Easter or the Trinity period, and she says this follows regional zones. Within the period one day carries the main rites, and she divides it into a preparation, a meeting of relatives at the cemetery, a walk among the graves, commemoration at the grave, and a continuation at home.

She finds these days both family occasions and social ones, with their importance held or growing, and says collective commemoration repairs ties weakened by distance and broken family traditions. The abstract does not name the day, and the counts of respondents are not given.

sections.heading: What the three sources do not settle
paras: The sources do not say where the folk days came from. A common account makes Radonitsa and Semik pagan spring feasts of the dead that the Church absorbed, but none of the three read here supports or refutes that, and the one popular essay on the subject that came up in searching was not used. What they show is narrower: two calendars that overlap, one the Church’s and one regional, and a regional practice that was moved toward the Church’s Saturdays.
The atlas therefore marks the origin question as contested and leaves it open. The calendar here is a table of who named which day, not a history of how the days arose.

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: No dates for any year are given: the days move with Easter and the sources do not.
Russian village practice before the twentieth century is not described. The Russian field evidence is from 2016–2017, the older evidence is four Komi-Permyak recordings.
Belarusian Dziady, rusalia, Maslenitsa and the Chuvash Simēk are left to plates with sources of their own.
Dates and customs found only on popular sites are not repeated.

items: No parish record, such as a parish chronicle or a priest’s register, was read for this plate, so the parish level is only the difference between the Church’s present rule and the 1913 reference work. A study of parish chronicles of Smolensk province (I. Pashkova, Vestnik antropologii, 2022) came up in searching and is a lead, not a source used here.
Zelenin’s account of Semik and the commemoration of the unnatural dead, read in the 1995 edition.

A source for the claim, seen only on popular sites, that the word Radonitsa is attested from the 14th century.

plates.title: TABOO, OMEN AND PROTECTION
plates.subtitle: Covered mirrors, thrown-out water and the reasons attached to them
plates.dek: What sources report people did in a house of mourning, which reasons are on record for each act, and where the reports do not agree. No customs are offered as rules.
plates.marginal: Two aims, eight acts, several reasons that do not agree. Nothing here is advice.
plates.period: Customs reported from earlier ethnography; fieldwork 2018–2019
plates.location: East Slavic villages; Russian North; Khislavichi district, Smolensk region
plates.tradition: Russian funeral custom and its protective and cleansing acts

sections.heading: Two aims, and the acts that serve them
paras: An encyclopedia article on East Slavic funeral rites says the rite works in two directions: some acts help the dead reach the other world, others protect the living from the dead. Its protective and cleansing acts include washing the house after the coffin is carried out, turning objects over, covering mirrors and washing hands on returning from the cemetery. Its prohibitions include close relatives making the coffin and bringing food back from the cemetery.

The explanation the article gives is general: the dead can harm the living, and the boundary between worlds stays open from the death until the burial and the fortieth day. It does not give a reason for each separate act, and it does not date its examples. The page does not name an author. The page has no bibliography, but it names its authorities in the text: Baiburin (1993), Razumova (2012), Tolstaya (2009, 2019), Spassky (1877) and an 1890 collection of materials on daily life. Washing as removal of the marks of the living is attributed to Baiburin; the epistolary character of laments in the Russian North to Tolstaya.

sections.heading: In the house
paras: J. Rouhier-Willoughby, in a review of urban funerals, lists what the older village rite is reported to have included: candles lit, all the mirrors in the house covered, all water thrown out. She says mirrors were thought symbolically close to water, which is why both were treated the same. The women who washed the body turned tables and benches over before washing them, she writes, so that death would enter the soil; a priest might also say a prayer of purification once the body had been carried out.
She draws these from earlier ethnographers, so the village custom reaches the atlas at second hand. For the urban twentieth century she reports that the covering of shiny surfaces continued.

sections.heading: Washing
paras: Washing the body appears in both sources as an obligatory part of the rite. The encyclopedia cites a scholar who argues that the strictness of the rule points to a purpose beyond cleaning: removing what marked the person as living. In the Russian North, it says, older women past childbearing were often hired to wash the dead.

In the Khislavichi district of Smolensk, A. Ryko’s informants said neighbours were invited to wash, women washing women and men washing men, and she found no stated ban on relatives taking part. Where the encyclopedia lists a prohibition, her district does not report it. The two sources describe different places and cannot be added together.

sections.heading: Done without an explanation
paras: Ryko writes that people in the borderland often perform funeral actions without being able to say what they are for, and that as the motives fade the sense of obligation fades with them. This is her observation of one district, based on informants’ memories, and she says it is unclear whether the trend is local.

It matters here because the reasons attached to protective acts in the other sources are the reasons collected from or ascribed to people at particular times. They are not a fixed meaning that every act always carried.

sections.heading: Why the mirror?
paras: Several reasons are on record for covering mirrors. A hieromonk, writing against the custom, reports that people said the soul should not be frightened by its reflection, or the dead should not frighten the family, or the soul might pass into the mirror. Rouhier-Willoughby, reporting scholarship, ties mirrors to water, which was also thrown out.

These do not agree with each other and none is shown here to be the original. The church writer is hostile and gives the folk reasons in order to dismiss them. The atlas lists the reasons and leaves the meaning of the act unsettled.

sections.heading: The Church’s position
paras: Hieromonk Dometian calls the covering of mirrors a folk custom with nothing in common with the Orthodox burial rite, and he says the same of overturning tables and chairs, which he calls pagan survivals. He also reports a belief that one must not look out of a window at a funeral procession, and he tells believers to take the blessing of a priest as their only guide.
This is a polemical text of unstated date. It shows what the Church objects to, and by implication what was practised, but it is not a count of practice.

plates.title: THE MATERIALS OF ABANDONMENT
plates.subtitle: Demolished cemeteries, gravestones as curbs and what is documented
plates.dek: Dated decisions reported from Siberia and a 2019 find in Moscow, with the larger historical claims marked unverified because the articles cite no documents.
plates.marginal: Two articles, one interview. The dates are reported, the motives are one reading, the metro filler is unverified.
plates.tradition: Soviet and post-Soviet treatment of cemeteries

sections.heading: Novosibirsk: dated decisions, as reported
paras: In a 2023 interview, E. Krasilnikova of Novosibirsk State Technical University dates a run of local decisions. A 1920 decision concerned cutting the grove at the cemetery. In 1929 the Voskresenskaya church was ordered closed, and in April 1930 a crowd of about a thousand protested and was dispersed by the militia. The old cemetery became a garden and later part of a park; the church went to the park administration, held a planetarium and burned in the 1970s.
She places the start of such demolitions in Siberia in the mid-1920s. The interview states the dates as facts but cites no file or archive for them, so they stand here as the interviewee’s report.

sections.heading: Barnaul and Omsk
paras: In her account two large cemeteries in Barnaul were destroyed in the 1930s, graves were opened for valuables and remains left scattered. She calls Barnaul the most radical case in Siberia; that comparison is her judgement.

Omsk went another way. She says its historic necropolis survived until the 1950s, was recorded and photographed by a museum director before its demolition, and in 2005 fragments of its stones were gathered into a memorial square. Novosibirsk has no comparable memorial, she adds.

sections.alt: A rusted iron grave fence and a fallen pale wooden cross among young birch and spruce, with blueberry scrub covering the ground and a collapsed wooden structure at the right
sections.caption: A fence and a fallen cross in an abandoned cemetery on Sredny Island, Keret Archipelago, 2023. The plate does not say why it was abandoned.

sections.heading: Curbs on a Moscow embankment, 2019
paras: A. Minkin reports that gravestones were found used as curbs near the Estrada Theatre on Bersenevskaya Embankment while the curbs were being replaced. The photographs came from a municipal deputy who posted them online, and some stones still showed dates of birth and death. The construction department told the outlet that the work was not under its direction. He also recalls a similar case from 2011 on Bolshaya Polyanka.

A second report, by BFM (17 October 2019), describes the same find as granite steps of the theatre, not curbs. It quotes A. Frolov of the Arkhnadzor council, who attributed one slab to the gravestone of Colonel Pyotr Beketov from the Novospassky Monastery and read the find as a trace of the clearing of old cemeteries in the 1930s. The two reports differ on what the stones were used as, and the attribution of the slab is one preservationist’s statement, not an inspection record.
The 2019 find is therefore known through a deputy’s photographs and an outlet’s report, not through an inspection record.

sections.heading: Claims with no document behind them
paras: The same article quotes an architect, S. Tkachenko, who says that reuse of granite for roads was normal in the 1920s and 1930s, that many stone buildings were demolished in 1934 and the rubble used as metro filler or concrete. The state enterprise ‘Ritual’ is quoted as saying the practice was common, that many cemeteries were cleared in the first half of the twentieth century for the metro and roads, with curbs at Sokolniki, Tverskoy Boulevard and Novaya Basmannaya Street, and that unused slabs were crushed into rubble.
No decision, order or archive is cited for any of this. The atlas keeps the statements and marks them UNVERIFIED: they are plausible, they come from named speakers, and they are not documented here.

sections.heading: Why the cemeteries went
paras: Krasilnikova gives four kinds of motive for the demolitions: ideological (shedding pre-revolutionary culture and building a socialist city), practical (neglected graves after the Civil War, typhus burials, no relatives left to tend them), symbolic (local notables buried there whom the new authorities saw no need to remember) and emotional (funerals used to mobilise people, revolutionary rites replacing religious ones).

These are her interpretations of Siberian cases and are not sourced in the interview. The atlas lists them as one reading, and does not give them as the cause of abandoned cemeteries elsewhere, including the one in the photograph.

plates.title: THE DIGITAL AFTERLIFE
plates.subtitle: Online memorials, accounts of the dead and what sources claim
plates.dek: Three sources on dead users’ accounts, online mourning and avatars of the dead, all read at the level of an abstract or a news item and stated as such.
plates.marginal: Three abstracts. A projection, an argument and a pair of claims, none of them a count.
plates.tradition: Online commemoration in Russia

sections.heading: More dead than living
paras: A. Sergeeva, R. Gerlit and H. Krcmar analysed 33 social networks and online services, surveyed 173 internet users and interviewed experts, taking Russia as their example. Their abstract expects services to host more deceased than living users in the coming decades, accounts and data to persist, the deceased to keep receiving invitations and birthday greetings, and heirs to find it hard to identify all accounts and reach the data.
This plate has the abstract only. The ‘more dead than living’ line is a projection, and the survey’s sample is not known here.

sections.heading: A dissertation on mourning online
paras: K. Linden’s doctoral dissertation at Uppsala studies online commemoration in the Russian-speaking world by virtual ethnography of three memorial sites, among them one on Soviet repressions and one on the Nord-Ost siege, together with social networking sites. She argues that online tools enable communal remembrance, that this has three sides (between the living and the dead, among mourners, and as motive for action), and that digitalisation may challenge a political culture of forgetting.

She also argues that the ‘right to be forgotten’ is not necessarily the answer, because difficulty in forgetting online could help repair a broken memory culture. This is an argument within her theoretical framework. The atlas has the library abstract only and treats it as her claim.

sections.heading: Avatars and grief
paras: Researchers from HSE University in Nizhny Novgorod, T. Khusyainov and E. Urusova, are reported as saying that digital footprints can support grief by sustaining a sense of connection, and that the same tools can raise anxiety, delay acceptance of loss and increase the risk of retraumatisation. They describe AI avatars of the dead, which can recreate voice and habits and can also produce errors, with a comparison to Frankenstein’s creature.
The two effects are put forward together by the researchers themselves, and the atlas leaves both open. The plate has a university news item, not the article. The item does not discuss Russian law.

sections.heading: What platforms say they do
paras: A news item reports that VKontakte marks or deletes the page of a dead user at the request of relatives, who send a photograph of the death certificate. If the page is kept, the words ‘Страница умершего человека’ appear in place of the last-visit time. The same item says that since 2011 a VK page could be kept unchanged or deleted, that Odnoklassniki adds a black ribbon or turns the photo black and white, and that Facebook has a ‘legacy contact’ and a memorial label.

This is a report of platform policy as of the item’s date, which the excerpt read does not show. The platforms’ own help pages were not read, and rules of this kind change. What the item shows is that a page of the dead is a category the platform has made a procedure for, with a document as the key.
